title: The Housing Theory of Everything
author: Sam Bowman, John Myers & Ben Southwood
blurb: Takes a dozen unrelated-looking problems and shows one constraint sitting under all of them. The reframe is the thing worth stealing, not the housing data.

title: Meditations on Moloch
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A name for the thing that happens when everyone acts rationally and the outcome is still terrible. Twelve years on it is still the vocabulary people reach for.

title: Reality Has a Surprising Amount of Detail
author: John Salvatier
blurb: The gap between reading about a thing and doing it is wider than anyone admits. A short piece that quietly rewires how you approach new skills.

title: The Bitter Lesson
author: Richard Sutton
blurb: Forty years of AI history compressed into one uncomfortable pattern: general methods that leverage computation beat clever human priors. Every hype cycle forgets it anyway.

title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Two incompatible calendars share one office. The essay that gave a generation permission to block their mornings and feel less guilty about it.

title: How to Do Great Work
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Graham's late-career synthesis: curiosity as compass, taste as filter, and the boring middle where most people quit. Long, but it earns the length.

title: Fast
author: Patrick Collison
blurb: A scrapbook of things that happened faster than you think they should have. Less argument than provocation — and the provocation lands.

title: The Tyranny of the Marginal User
author: Ivan Vendrov
blurb: Why your favourite app keeps getting worse: growth metrics select for the person who churns over the person who cares. A diagnosis without a cure, which is honest.

title: I Should Have Loved Biology
author: James Somers
blurb: Somers on how textbooks kill the subject they are meant to teach. The best case for rewriting science pedagogy from first principles.

title: You and Your Research
author: Richard Hamming
blurb: Hamming asking the room why they are not working on important problems — and meaning it. Still uncomfortable in the best way.

title: A Big Little Idea Called Legibility
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Scott's monoculture, Le Corbusier's grid, and the urge to make the world readable to planners. The essay that launched a thousand critiques of optimisation.

title: The Rise and Fall of Peer Review
author: Adam Mastroianni
blurb: Peer review was never the gold standard — it was a workaround that became sacred. Mastroianni makes the history funny and the implications hard to ignore.

title: How Complex Systems Fail
author: Richard Cook
blurb: Eighteen tight propositions on why accidents are normal, not anomalous. Required reading for anyone who builds things that can hurt people.

title: The Copenhagen Interpretation of Ethics
author: Jai Dhyani
blurb: Once you engage with a problem, you become blameworthy for every part of it you fail to fix. A sharp coinage for a familiar trap.

title: Slack
author: Zvi Mowshowitz
blurb: The case for leaving room in systems — budgets, schedules, organisations — so they can absorb surprise. Efficiency has a hidden tax.

title: Things You're Allowed to Do
author: Milan Cvitkovic
blurb: A list of ordinary liberties people forget they have — calling the author, skipping the meeting, renegotiating the lease. Permission slips as genre.

title: The Cook and the Chef
author: Tim Urban
blurb: Reasoning from first principles versus reasoning by analogy, told with stick figures and surprising teeth. Urban at his most useful.

title: It's Time to Build
author: Marc Andreessen
blurb: A pandemic-era sermon on institutional sclerosis and the moral case for making things. Agree or not, it named a mood.

title: Why We Stopped Making Einsteins
author: Erik Hoel
blurb: Hoel's case that the pipeline for eccentric brilliance has been dismantled by credentialism and narrow apprenticeship. Provocative even where you disagree.

title: Why Books Don't Work
author: Andy Matuschak
blurb: Books transfer words, not understanding — and the medium has never been designed to close that gap. A quiet challenge to how we read.

title: Do Things That Don't Scale
author: Paul Graham
blurb: The counterintuitive early playbook: do things manually, embarrassingly, one user at a time. The advice YC founders still quote.

title: How to Make Wealth
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Wealth is not money; it is stuff people want. Graham's clearest statement of what startups actually produce.

title: Startup = Growth
author: Paul Graham
blurb: A startup is a company designed to grow fast — and that definition has consequences for everything else.

title: How to Get Startup Ideas
author: Paul Graham
blurb: The best ideas look like toys and start as problems you have yourself. A field guide to not chasing fake opportunities.

title: Be Good
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Why being good is not just moral but strategic — and how arseholes eventually tax themselves out of the network.

title: What You Can't Say
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Every era has opinions that cannot be stated without social cost. Finding them is a map to where thinking is stuck.

title: Hackers and Painters
author: Paul Graham
blurb: What hackers and painters share: making things, taste, and the gap between what you imagined and what you built.

title: Cities and Ambition
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Different cities whisper different ambitions at you. A piece that explains why geography still matters for builders.

title: Why Nerds Are Unpopular
author: Paul Graham
blurb: A theory of high-school status that doubles as a memoir of being the wrong kind of clever in the wrong place.

title: Life is Short
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Bullshit is the thing that expands to fill the time you forget is finite. Short enough to reread annually.

title: How to Think for Yourself
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Independent-mindedness is not innate — it is a set of habits you can steal from people who have them.

title: Keep Your Identity Small
author: Paul Graham
blurb: The more labels you wear, the harder it is to change your mind. A one-sentence test for intellectual stuckness.

title: The Bus Ticket Theory of Genius
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Maybe genius is mostly obsessive interest applied over time, not a lottery ticket you are born holding.

title: Schlep Blindness
author: Paul Graham
blurb: The best opportunities hide behind tedious, unglamorous work everyone else avoids. You cannot see them until you look.

title: How to Disagree
author: Paul Graham
blurb: A hierarchy of disagreement that turns Twitter fights into a taxonomy. Still the best reply to bad-faith dunking.

title: The Age of the Essay
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Essays are how you figure things out, not just report what you know. A manifesto for the form this app is built on.

title: What I Worked On
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Graham's autobiography in essay form — Lisp, Viaweb, YC, Hacker News. The through-line is curiosity with deadlines.

title: Default Alive or Default Dead
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Two questions that cut through startup delusion: are you default alive or default dead, and do you know which?

title: Mean People Fail
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Meanness is not strength; it is a tax on cooperation that compounds. A note to founders who confuse fear with respect.

title: Writing, Briefly
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Write simply, revise brutally, read aloud. Graham's compressed guide to prose that does not waste the reader's time.

title: The Refragmentation
author: Paul Graham
blurb: America was more equal when it was more uniform — and the unraveling of that uniformity has complicated politics ever since.

title: Having Kids
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Honest and unsentimental notes on what children cost and what they give back. Rare in the genre.

title: What Doesn't Seem Like Work
author: Paul Graham
blurb: The thing that feels like play to you and work to others is probably your comparative advantage. Find it early.

title: General and Surprising
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Good startup ideas are general enough to grow and surprising enough that most people dismiss them at first.

title: The Top Idea in Your Mind
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Whatever sits at the top of your mental stack drives outcomes more than you notice. Guard that slot carefully.

title: I Can Tolerate Anything Except the Outgroup
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Tolerance is easy toward people who agree with you on the important thing — which is usually not the stated thing.

title: Beware the Man of One Study
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: One paper is a hint, not a worldview. The essay that should be stapled to every hot take citing a single RCT.

title: The Control Group Is Out Of Control
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: When the control group performs miracles, maybe your model of evidence needs updating. Weird, funny, and unsettling.

title: Who By Very Slow Decay
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A harrowing tour of end-of-life care that makes the abstract debate about death panels unbearably concrete.

title: Considerations on Cost Disease
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Why does everything — healthcare, education, housing — cost more while TVs get cheaper? A patient survey of the suspects.

title: The Categories Were Made For Man, Not Man For The Categories
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: When reality outruns the labels, do you fix the labels or punish the reality? A parable about classification and compassion.

title: Against Individual IQ Worries
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Obsessing over your own IQ is both pointless and corrosive. A permission slip to stop ranking yourself on the wrong axis.

title: Radicalizing the Romanceless
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A uncomfortable map of how chronic rejection can slide into ideology. Whether you buy the frame, the mechanism is worth understanding.

title: The Tails Coming Apart As Metaphor For Life
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: When two things correlate in the middle but diverge at the extremes, arguments that conflate them fall apart. A statistical fable.

title: The Goddess of Everything Else
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A parable about Moloch's opposite — the god of everything sacrificed to win one thing. Strange and oddly moving.

title: Book Review: Twelve Rules For Life
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: The Peterson review everyone argued about — fair where it should be, sharp where it needs to be, funny throughout.

title: How The West Was Won
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: A case that the modern world is weirdly, specifically good — and that pretending otherwise wastes the advantage.

title: Against Murderism
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: If you expand a word until it covers everyone you dislike, it stops doing moral work. A plea for narrower definitions.

title: The Non-Libertarian FAQ
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Steel-man objections to libertarianism without the usual bad faith. Long, but it earns trust by arguing fairly.

title: Untitled
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: On the gap between the person you perform and the person you are. Short, oblique, and stuck in memory.

title: Social Criticism As Esoteric Skill
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Complaining well is a craft most people never learn — and bad social criticism has predictable failure modes.

title: What Developmental Milestones Are You Missing?
author: Scott Alexander
blurb: Childhood used to teach skills adults now lack — and the absence shows up in politics, work, and relationships.

title: The Gervais Principle
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: The Office as org-chart ethnography: sociopaths, clueless, and losers in a theory too honest for HR.

title: Welcome to the Future Nauseous
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: We can only inhabit the future in small doses before nausea sets in. Why most 'visionary' talk fails the stomach test.

title: The American Cloud
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Data centers as sovereign islands in the American landscape — a travelogue of where the cloud actually lives.

title: A Brief History of the Corporation: 1600 to 2100
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: The corporation as a time-bounded technology, not a permanent fixture. Speculative history that clarifies the present.

title: The Premium Mediocre Life of Maya Millennial
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Premium mediocre: the aesthetic of seeming affluent while renting everything. A coinage that spread because it was true.

title: The Calculus of Grit
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Grit is not blind persistence — it is knowing which failures to absorb and which to abandon. A more adult version of the virtue.

title: The Extended Brain Hypothesis
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Your brain was never just in your skull; tools extend cognition. A frame for understanding note-taking and AI assistants alike.

title: Be Slightly Evil
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: Not cartoon villainy — just enough willingness to play the game that nice people pretend does not exist.

title: The Streetlight Effect
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: You search where the light is, not where you lost the keys. A parable about metrics and misplaced rigor.

title: The Art of Gig
author: Venkatesh Rao
blurb: The gig economy as a design problem for individual operators — not just a labour-market trend to lament.

title: Timing Technology
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: When will a technology actually matter? Gwern's methodical answer to a question everyone guesses at badly.

title: The Melancholy of Subculture Society
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: Subcultures were supposed to save us from mass culture. Instead they became another thing to consume and leave.

title: Silk Road 1
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: An archival deep dive into the first darknet market — part true crime, part lesson in how online communities evolve.

title: Spaced Repetition
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: The most evidence-backed study hack, explained with Gwern's usual obsessive completeness. Long, but it replaces a dozen shorter posts.

title: Claude Shannon
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: Shannon as he actually worked: playful, restless, and uninterested in fame. A portrait of a mind that invented a field then wandered off.

title: On Seeing Everything
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: What happens when nothing is scarce except attention and everything is archived forever.

title: Open Questions
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: A living list of questions Gwern wishes someone would answer. Reading it makes your own curiosity feel underemployed.

title: Blackmail
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: Blackmail as a weird corner of mechanism design — morally fraught, economically fascinating, thoroughly Gwern.

title: Modafinil
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: Self-experimentation as epistemology: one person's years-long trial of a cognitive enhancer, reported with uncomfortable honesty.

title: Bitcoin Is Worse Is Better
author: Gwern Branwen
blurb: Why the ugly, limited version of a technology sometimes wins. Bitcoin through the lens of Gabriel's Worse is Better.

title: Computer latency: 1977-2017
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Your phone is slower than a thirty-year-old workstation at some tasks. A benchmark that shames the industry.

title: Why hardware development is hard
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Hardware looks easy until you try to ship it. Luu on iteration cycles, tooling gaps, and why software people underestimate the field.

title: Web bloat
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Today's web pages are megabytes to show a paragraph. A side-by-side that makes the bloat impossible to unsee.

title: How I learned to program
author: Dan Luu
blurb: No bootcamp fairy tale — just what actually worked and what wasted time. Refreshingly unsentimental.

title: Normalization of deviance
author: Dan Luu
blurb: How teams learn to accept broken norms until disaster snaps them back. The Challenger essay for software and ops.

title: Keyboard latency
author: Dan Luu
blurb: You can feel lag you cannot measure until someone measures it for you. A case study in hidden friction.

title: Is dev compensation bimodal?
author: Dan Luu
blurb: The claim that developer pay splits into two humps is mostly a statistical artefact. Luu punctures a popular anxiety.

title: How web bloat affects users with slow devices
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Fast laptops hide the cost of bloated sites; slow phones pay it. A reminder that your users are not your machine.

title: Programming languages as part of a system stack
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Language speed matters less than where the language sits in the stack — until suddenly it matters enormously.

title: Why's that company so big?
author: Dan Luu
blurb: Size is not always moat — sometimes it is legacy, regulation, or inertia. A short checklist for scepticism.

title: Status as a Service
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: Social networks sell status the way games sell points — and the token economics explain more than the feature lists.

title: Invisible Asymptotes
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: Every product hits a ceiling it cannot see until it hits it. Wei on Amazon, Facebook, and the limits that hide in plain sight.

title: Amazon's Flywheel
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: The flywheel metaphor done properly — not as diagram decoration but as an operating logic you can test against.

title: Seeing Like an Algorithm
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: Algorithms do not see what humans see — they see proxies, and people learn to perform the proxies. Scott applied to feeds.

title: American Idle
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: On unemployment, stimulus, and what 'idle' means in an economy that measures the wrong things.

title: Compress to Impress
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: TikTok's compression of story into seconds is not dumbing down — it is a new grammar of impressing quickly.

title: The TikTok Strategy
author: Eugene Wei
blurb: How recommendation-first feeds change what gets made. The essay that made product people take TikTok seriously.

title: Aggregation Theory
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: The lens for understanding Google, Facebook, and Netflix: aggregate demand, own the customer, dictate terms to suppliers.

title: The End of the Beginning
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: The consumer internet's growth phase is over; what comes next is harder and weirder. Thompson's era-defining piece.

title: Defining Aggregators
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: Not every big tech company is an aggregator — and mislabeling them sends you to the wrong playbook.

title: The Great Unbundling
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: Newspapers sold a bundle; the internet unbundled it and kept the profitable parts. A post-mortem still relevant.

title: Tech's Two Philosophies
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: Apple's humanism versus Google's utilitarianism — a split that explains product choices better than specs do.

title: The Super-Aggregators
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: When an aggregator aggregates aggregators, regulation gets hard and competition gets weird.

title: The Internet and the Third Estate
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: From printing press to podcast: every revolution in distribution reshapes who gets to speak and who must listen.

title: The Amazon Tax
author: Ben Thompson
blurb: AWS as tax on the internet economy — and the strategic moat that funds everything else Amazon tries.

title: Newspapers and Thinking the Unthinkable
author: Clay Shirky
blurb: Revolutions do not happen when society adopts new tools — they happen when society adopts new tools and old institutions cannot adapt.

title: Gin, Television, and Social Surplus
author: Clay Shirky
blurb: We had a cognitive surplus; we spent it on sitcoms. The internet offered something else to do with free time.

title: The Collapse of Complex Business Models
author: Clay Shirky
blurb: When the environment changes, complexity that once was strength becomes fatal weight. A post-mortem template.

title: Here Comes Everybody
author: Clay Shirky
blurb: How groups form when coordinating gets cheap — and why that breaks institutions built for expensive coordination.

title: Metacrap
author: Cory Doctorow
blurb: Everything you know about metadata is wrong, and the people selling it know that. Twenty years on, still quoted.

title: The Internet Con
author: Cory Doctorow
blurb: How enshittification works as a business model — and why 'just vote with your feet' is not a plan.

title: Why I Won't Buy an iPad
author: Cory Doctorow
blurb: A forecast of walled-garden computing framed as a personal purchase decision. Prescient and still irritating to fans.

title: Doctorow's First Law
author: Cory Doctorow
blurb: Any time someone says intermediaries are obsolete, they are selling you something that needs an intermediary.

title: A Brief History & Ethnography of LLMs
author: Maggie Appleton
blurb: LLMs as cultural artefacts, not just tools — mapped with Appleton's usual visual intelligence.

title: The Dark Forest Theory of the Internet
author: Maggie Appleton
blurb: Public speech online attracts predators; the wise retreat to private groves. A metaphor that names post-social-media behaviour.

title: Digital Gardeners
author: Maggie Appleton
blurb: The history of tending a personal website like a garden — unfinished, linked, alive. A manifesto for this app's aesthetic cousins.

title: Tools for Thought
author: Maggie Appleton
blurb: A visual tour of note-taking cults and their promises. Skeptical without being cynical.

title: The Garden and the Stream
author: Maggie Appleton
blurb: Ephemeral streams versus cultivated gardens — two metaphors for what the web could be.

title: Looking for Alice
author: Henrik Karlsson
blurb: On finding a person, not a type — and how optimisation culture makes both harder. Tender and unusually honest.

title: On not being a normie
author: Henrik Karlsson
blurb: What it means to live slightly off the modal life path — without turning difference into a personality.

title: How to find a good partner
author: Henrik Karlsson
blurb: Not listicle advice — a theory of compatibility that takes temperament and context seriously.

title: Why we can't have nice things
author: Henrik Karlsson
blurb: Nice things require shared standards and long horizons — both in short supply. A lament with structure.

title: The Most Precious Resource is Agency
author: Simon Sarris
blurb: Schools train compliance; the world rewards people who can act without permission. A case for protecting agency early.

title: How to Live an Intellectually Rich Life
author: Simon Sarris
blurb: Breadth, slack, and seriousness — not hacks. Sarris on building a mind that stays interesting after university.

title: The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge
author: Simon Sarris
blurb: Abraham Flexner updated for people who feel guilty reading outside their lane. Permission to wander.

title: On Self-Respect
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Self-respect is a discipline, not a mood — and once lost it is hard to borrow from someone else. Didion at her most precise.

title: Goodbye to All That
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Leaving New York as a moral decision, not a geographic one. The template for every later 'I quit the city' essay.

title: The White Album
author: Joan Didion
publication: The New York Review of Books
blurb: The sixties did not hold together as a story — Didion reports from inside the fracture. Journalism as literature.

title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
author: Joan Didion
blurb: Haight-Ashbury without romance — Didion watching a scene realize it has no centre.

title: Politics and the English Language
author: George Orwell
blurb: Bad prose and bad politics share habits — vagueness, passive voice, ready-made phrases. Still the best editing checklist with stakes.

title: Why I Write
author: George Orwell
blurb: Four motives for writing — sheer egoism, aesthetic enthusiasm, historical impulse, political purpose — and how they fight.

title: Cargo Cult Science
author: Richard Feynman
blurb: The difference between looking scientific and being scientific — told with Feynman's impatient warmth.

title: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years
author: Peter Norvig
blurb: The book title is a lie; expertise takes a decade. Norvig's polite demolition of shortcut culture.

title: The Angel's Thesis
author: James Somers
blurb: On sentences that carry more weight than their length suggests — and how to notice them when you read.

title: Six Months in a Leaky Boat
author: James Somers
blurb: Inside the world of quantified-self startups — Somers reporting before he became the essayist developers quote.

title: Taming the Mammoth
author: Tim Urban
blurb: Social approval as a prehistoric beast riding your decisions. Pop psychology that accidentally helps.

title: Science Is Broken. Here's How to Fix It.
author: Adam Mastroianni
blurb: Not just critique — actual proposals for making science less performative. Mastroianni at his most constructive.

title: Things I Believe
author: Adam Mastroianni
blurb: A numbered list of convictions stated plainly enough to disagree with. Refreshing in a genre of hedged manifestos.

title: Questions
author: Patrick Collison
blurb: A list of open questions worth working on — less answer than invitation. Collison's taste on display.

title: How to Build a Better Social Network
author: Ivan Vendrov
blurb: Concrete mechanisms for healthier online community — rare in a genre of hand-wringing.

title: Play in Hard Mode
author: Zvi Mowshowitz
blurb: Easy mode teaches the wrong lessons; hard mode is how you actually level up. Game metaphors that earn their keep.

title: A Lesson in Safe Design
author: Richard Cook
blurb: Safety is an emergent property of systems, not a component you bolt on. Cook compresses a career into one anecdote.

title: The Present Situation of Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell
blurb: Russell clearing ground for analytic philosophy — dense, but the opening chapters repay the climb.

title: Consider the Lobster
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: A food festival assignment that becomes a serious question about suffering — and about what journalism can ask.

title: A Supposedly Fun Thing I'll Never Do Again
author: David Foster Wallace
blurb: A cruise ship as American excess laboratory — Wallace funny, miserable, and precise in equal measure.

title: The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction
author: Walter Benjamin
blurb: Reproduction changes aura — Benjamin's lens for thinking about copies, memes, and AI slop alike.

title: The Hedgehog and the Fox
author: Isaiah Berlin
blurb: One big idea versus many small ones — a typology for thinkers that also describes how you read.

title: The Problem of Social Cost
author: Ronald Coase
blurb: Rights and liabilities get assigned to minimise total cost — the foundation of law-and-economics in one paper.

title: The Banality of Evil
author: Hannah Arendt
blurb: Eichmann as bureaucrat, not monster — the report that argued evil could be ordinary and infuriated everyone.

title: The Power Broker
author: Robert Caro
blurb: How Robert Moses reshaped New York without ever winning an election — an excerpt that reads like a thriller.
